source_scope: 34 non-archived TheAlgorithms algorithm repositories. Portable-language source paths can supply benchmark implementations; AArch64 Assembly paths are included only as discovery references.
matching_method: Normalize each source filename stem (including camelCase to snake_case); Project Euler solN files include their problem number. Identical normalized stems are candidate matches only and have not been checked for equivalent behavior. Candidates may declare benchmark_name when a numeric or otherwise non-descriptive source stem needs an alphabetic algorithm folder, and additional_benchmark_names when one source candidate contains multiple distinct benchmarkable algorithms.
excluded_paths: Tests, examples, benchmarks, documentation, scripts, build output, and vendor directories are omitted.

source_repositories.usage: discovery reference only; architecture-specific assembly is not a portable benchmark implementation

candidates.review_notes: The pinned Dart source uses the direct recursive include-or-exclude recurrence without memoization. It is kept distinct from the bottom-up tabulation benchmark so their runtime and call-stack behavior can be compared. The shared contract bounds the item count to 16 to keep the exponential recurrence practical and defines malformed inputs explicitly.

The pinned Jupyter notebook is an end-to-end Keras IMDB sentiment-classification workflow: it loads a remote dataset, trains a neural network, evaluates it, and plots results. It is not a standalone deterministic algorithm with a bounded callable input/output contract, so it is excluded from the benchmark catalog.

The pinned C++ source fills a bottom-up 0/1 knapsack table with the same item/capacity recurrence as the canonical tabulation candidate. This filename is retained as an alias to share one workload and contract.

The pinned C LeetCode source solves the Two Sum problem with nested scans under the source problem's single-solution assumption. It overwrites the result for each matching pair, so multiple matches select the last pair in scan order, and a no-solution input returns a zero-filled pair. The shared benchmark defines an explicit no-pair sentinel and a deterministic earliest-pair rule; this numeric filename is reviewed as an alias of that standardized Two Sum contract.

The pinned C LeetCode source performs recursive full-string matching with '.' for one character and '*' for zero or more repetitions of its preceding atom. It has the same matching semantics as the Python recursive_match implementation and aliases that contract.

The pinned C LeetCode 1008 source recursively partitions a valid BST preorder at each root and constructs left and right subtrees. The shared contract validates unique signed 32-bit keys, bounds the input to 15 nodes, and emits an explicit preorder tree serialization with null markers.

The pinned C LeetCode 1009 source complements the significant bits of a nonnegative integer using a logarithmic bit-length calculation. C LeetCode 476 uses the same mask semantics. The shared benchmark uses integer shifts, handles zero explicitly, and bounds inputs to the source signed 32-bit domain.

The pinned C LeetCode 101 source recursively compares mirrored node pairs. Its behavior matches the canonical Python symmetric_tree source and Java CheckTreeIsSymmetric source; this numeric filename is recorded as an alias of symmetric_tree.

The pinned C LeetCode source scans the remaining linked list from each node and records the first strictly greater value, defaulting to zero when no later node qualifies. This is an O(n^2) forward-scan algorithm. The shared contract bounds the list to 4,096 positive signed 32-bit values and serializes one result per node as little-endian bytes.

The pinned C LeetCode source recursively tracks the minimum and maximum value on each root-to-node path and updates the maximum absolute difference. The shared benchmark uses a bounded indexed-tree contract and portable implementations in all nine target languages.

The pinned C LeetCode source returns zero for a null tree and otherwise recursively returns one plus the larger child depth. The shared contract uses an indexed binary tree and portable recursive implementations in all nine target languages.

The pinned C LeetCode 108 implementation recursively selects the midpoint of the sorted input, allocates that key, and builds left and right subtrees; an empty input returns a null tree. The shared contract names the algorithm sorted_array_to_bst, requires strictly increasing signed 32-bit keys, uses the lower median for even ranges, and serializes the tree in preorder with null markers.

The pinned C LeetCode 1089 source copies the fixed-length array, then writes each original value and a second zero slot when needed; the output remains the original length. The shared contract accepts values 0 through 1,000, validates a bounded array, and serializes the transformed fixed-length result.

The pinned C LeetCode 109 source recursively uses slow and fast linked-list pointers to select each subtree root; this walk chooses the upper middle for even-sized sublists. The shared contract supplies the sorted list values as an array, accepts nondecreasing signed 32-bit sequences, and serializes the balanced tree in preorder.

The pinned C LeetCode 11 source implements the two-pointer maximum-container-area algorithm. The shared contract accepts nonnegative signed 32-bit heights and returns the maximum area as signed 64-bit; invalid heights and lengths are rejected.

The pinned C LeetCode source computes each node's left and right heights, then recursively checks both child subtrees; null trees are balanced. The benchmark preserves that repeated-height recursive approach under a bounded indexed-tree contract in all nine target languages.

The pinned C LeetCode 112 function recursively subtracts each node value from the requested sum and succeeds only at a leaf. The shared contract packs an indexed binary tree with a signed 64-bit target, validates that every node is reachable exactly once from root index 0, and returns whether any root-to-leaf path matches.
The pinned C LeetCode implementation uses T(0)=0, T(1)=1, T(2)=1 and the same nth-term recurrence as the canonical tribonacci benchmark.

The pinned C LeetCode 1147 candidate recursively peels matching prefix and suffix chunks and counts a remaining center chunk. The shared contract accepts 0 to 128 ASCII byte values in 1..127 and returns the maximum number of chunks; invalid input returns -1.
The pinned C LeetCode 118 source generates the first numRows rows of Pascal’s triangle, matching the canonical coefficient sequence.

The pinned C LeetCode 1184 function sums the distances on the two arcs between the selected stops and returns the smaller sum. The shared contract packs endpoint indices before 1 to 64 nonnegative distances bounded at 1,000,000.

The pinned C LeetCode 1189 candidate counts lowercase ASCII letters and returns the minimum of b, a, l/2, o/2, and n. The shared contract accepts 0 to 256 lowercase ASCII byte values and returns -1 for invalid input.

The pinned C LeetCode 119 source builds the requested zero-based Pascal-triangle row in place, updating interior coefficients from right to left. The shared contract bounds the row index to 0 through 33, matching its 32-bit coefficient domain, and serializes coefficients as little-endian unsigned 32-bit values.
The pinned C LeetCode filename 12 implements integer-to-Roman conversion for the standard 1 through 3,999 range. It aliases the descriptive integer_to_roman benchmark.

The pinned C LeetCode 1207 candidate sorts bounded occurrence counts and rejects duplicate positive frequencies. The shared contract accepts 0 to 1,000 values in -1,000..1,000; invalid input returns -1.

The pinned C LeetCode source computes the maximum subarray sum over adjacent price differences with Kadane's algorithm. This is equivalent to the single-buy/single-sell maximum-profit contract and aliases the shared stock benchmark.

The pinned C source implements the same recursive maximum-path-sum recurrence as the Python candidate binary_tree_maximum_path_sum. Its LOWER_BOUND declaration is missing a semicolon; the benchmark ports implement the evident intended algorithm.

The pinned C LeetCode 125 source uses inward-moving indices, skips non-alphanumeric characters, and compares ASCII letters without case sensitivity. The shared contract makes classification explicitly ASCII and uses a length-prefixed sequence of code points.

The pinned C LeetCode 1283 candidate binary-searches the least divisor whose rounded quotient sum meets the threshold. The shared contract packs the threshold before 1 to 256 positive values bounded at 1,000,000; thresholds below the item count return -1.

The pinned C LeetCode 13 source converts standard Roman symbols using additive values and subtracts I, X, or C before their valid higher pairs. It aliases the canonical Roman decoder under its uppercase 1 through 3,999 contract.
The pinned C LeetCode source XORs all signed 32-bit values, which returns the single value when every other value occurs twice. It aliases the shared single_number XOR contract.

The pinned C LeetCode filename 14 contains findMaxConsecutiveOnes, which counts contiguous nonzero values. On the standardized binary domain this is the maximum-consecutive-ones algorithm, so candidate 14 aliases max_consecutive_ones.

The pinned C LeetCode 141 source uses Floyd’s tortoise and hare pointers to report whether the list reachable from the head contains a cycle. The portable contract represents each next pointer as a signed node index, uses -1 for null and node 0 as the head, and returns 1 for a cycle, 0 for an acyclic path, or -1 for malformed input.

The pinned C LeetCode 142 source first finds a Floyd tortoise-and-hare meeting point, then advances one pointer from the head and one from the meeting point to locate the cycle entry. The portable contract uses successor indices with -1 for null and node 0 as the head, returning the zero-based entry index, -1 for an acyclic path, or -2 for malformed input.
The pinned C LeetCode 1524 candidate counts subarrays with odd sums using prefix parities. The shared contract accepts 0 to 100,000 signed 32-bit values and returns the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

The pinned C LeetCode 153 source compares the midpoint with the high endpoint and narrows the search interval to the minimum. The shared contract preserves the source assumption of a nonempty rotation of a strictly increasing array and bounds the input to 256 signed 64-bit values.

The pinned C LeetCode 16 source sorts the values and uses a two-pointer scan for the closest three-value sum. Its qsort mutates the input and its int difference calculation can overflow outside the original narrow problem bounds. The shared contract copies and heapsorts signed 32-bit values, widens sums and distance calculations to signed 64-bit, defines lower-sum tie resolution, and bounds the item count to 512.

The pinned C LeetCode 160 source advances two pointers and switches each to the other list head after reaching the end, returning the shared node pointer or null. The shared contract encodes pointer identity as nonnegative node IDs in two acyclic lists with aligned shared suffixes; nine portable ports preserve the O(m+n) head-switching traversal.

The pinned C LeetCode 1653 candidate uses a linear two-state dynamic program to minimize deletions that leave all a characters before all b characters. The shared contract packs a as 0 and b as 1, accepts up to 256 symbols, and returns -1 for invalid symbols or excess length.

The pinned C LeetCode 1657 candidate checks equal lowercase character sets and compares sorted occurrence counts. The shared contract packs two strings, each up to 256 lowercase ASCII bytes, after their lengths.
The pinned C LeetCode 169 source uses Boyer-Moore cancellation for the strict majority candidate. It matches the C-Sharp canonical algorithm; this numeric filename is recorded as an alias.

The pinned C LeetCode 1695 candidate uses a last-occurrence sliding window to maximize the sum of a contiguous subarray with distinct values. The shared contract accepts 0 to 256 values in 1..10,000 and returns -1 for invalid values or excess length.
The pinned C LeetCode 17 source emits the standard 2–9 keypad Cartesian product in the same order as the canonical phone-letter-combinations benchmark.
The pinned C LeetCode 1704 candidate counts vowels in equal string halves. The shared contract accepts even-length ASCII letter arrays up to 256 bytes and returns -1 for odd lengths or invalid bytes.

The pinned C LeetCode 173 source counts BST nodes, recursively materializes an in-order values array, then implements next by advancing an index and hasNext by checking whether a value remains. The shared indexed-tree contract returns an order-sensitive checksum for the full iterator trace; nine portable ports preserve eager materialization and sequential consumption.

The pinned C LeetCode 1752 candidate detects at most one descending adjacent pair in the circular array. The shared contract accepts 0 to 256 signed 32-bit values and returns -1 for invalid values or excess length.

The pinned C LeetCode 1769 candidate computes all per-box move distances in two linear passes. The shared contract accepts 0 to 256 binary occupancy values and serializes one unsigned 16-bit little-endian move count per box; invalid values, excess length, and insufficient capacity have explicit results.

The pinned C LeetCode 1833 candidate sorts positive bar costs, then greedily buys the cheapest bars while the budget allows. The shared contract packs a budget followed by up to 256 costs, with explicit ranges and invalid-input behavior.

The pinned C LeetCode 1838 candidate sorts values and uses a sliding window with prefix sums to find the largest group that can be raised to one value within budget. The shared contract packs budget and up to 256 values into one array and defines portable bounds and invalid-input behavior.

The pinned C LeetCode 189 source performs k right rotations by moving the last array value to index zero and shifting all preceding values one place on each pass. The shared contract defines signed 32-bit values, k from 0 through 1,024, and separate little-endian output; nine portable ports preserve the repeated-shift method.

The pinned C LeetCode 19 source counts nodes, walks to the predecessor of the one-based position from the tail, unlinks that node, and returns the updated head. It assumes the position is valid; this candidate aliases the Python remove_nth_node_from_end_of_list candidate under the shared bounded-list contract.

C LeetCode 190 explicitly reverses all 32 positions of an unsigned word, matching the Java, Python, and Rust reverse_bits sources. It is recorded as an alias of the shared fixed-width bit-reversal contract.

The pinned C LeetCode 191 source counts set bits across an unsigned 32-bit value. The C++ count_of_set_bits and JavaScript BinaryCountSetBits sources have the same result on this shared domain. The benchmark accepts the value through a signed 64-bit ABI, counts valid values from 0 through 2^32-1, and returns -1 outside that range.

Both pinned R files implement bottom-up 0/1 knapsack dynamic programming: one exposes a full table with item backtracking and a descending one-row space-optimized form, and the other also includes the same full-table and optimized recurrence. Their maximum-value result matches the shared 0/1 tabulation benchmark, so this candidate is an alias rather than a new algorithm.

The pinned C LeetCode 2 source adds the two least-significant-first digit lists node by node, propagates carry, and allocates one result node per processed digit including a final carry. The shared byte-output contract encodes both lists in one packed input and serializes result digits least-significant first.

The pinned C LeetCode 20 source uses a stack for matching parentheses, square brackets, and braces. Its stack semantics match the Java ValidParentheses candidate; this numeric filename is recorded as an alias of valid_parentheses.

The pinned C LeetCode 201 source clears the least significant set bit of the upper endpoint with n &= n - 1 until it equals the lower endpoint. The shared contract accepts inclusive nonnegative ranges through INT32_MAX and returns -1 for invalid bounds. Nine portable ports preserve the endpoint bit-clearing algorithm.

The pinned C LeetCode 2024 source runs a sliding window for each answer character, T and F, allowing at most k changes to the other character. The shared contract packs k followed by 0/1 answer values, limits sequences to 1,024 entries, and returns the longest run for either target.

The pinned C LeetCode 203 source recursively removes every node matching the target and returns the possibly changed head. The shared benchmark builds an index-based link chain, recursively rewrites retained-node links, and serializes surviving signed 32-bit values in list order.

The pinned AArch64 source is an interactive Linux terminal game rather than a standalone algorithm entry point. It includes architecture-specific termios, signal, poll, keyboard, random tile-spawn, display, and replay code. Extracting only its directional move kernels would be a new subalgorithm contract and would not cover this full program candidate, so it is excluded from the portable benchmark inventory.

The pinned C LeetCode 206 source iteratively reverses a singly linked list by redirecting each next pointer to the previous node. The linked-list operation trace now includes opcode 7 for this in-place reversal; all nine ports pass the extended trace oracle.

The pinned C LeetCode 2095 source counts the list, then uses fast and slow pointers plus the node-count parity to unlink the floor(n / 2)-indexed node; empty and singleton lists return an empty list. The shared indexed-link benchmark preserves the count pass, fast/slow traversal, unlink, and ordered signed 32-bit serialization.

The pinned C LeetCode 21 file contains iterative and recursive definitions of the same function; the benchmark selects its iterative linear two-pointer merge. The shared contract bounds both inputs to a combined 1,024 signed 32-bit values, validates sorted order, and serializes the merged ascending result.

The pinned C LeetCode 2125 source counts devices in each row, skips empty rows without resetting the previous nonempty count, and adds the product for every adjacent pair of nonempty rows. No existing benchmark has this grid-counting contract. The nine portable ports use a fixed-width row-major ASCII encoding.

The pinned C LeetCode 2130 source first copies linked-list values into an array, then scans mirrored indices in the first half and returns the largest pair sum. The contract preserves the source problem’s even list length and positive values from 1 through 100,000. No existing benchmark covers maximum mirrored-pair sums.

The pinned C LeetCode 215 source sorts the complete array in descending order with qsort and returns rank k - 1. This full-sort strategy is distinct from the Python candidate kth_largest_element, which uses iterative Lomuto quickselect, and is benchmarked separately.

The pinned C LeetCode 217 source sorts the integer array and scans adjacent values. The shared contract accepts up to 1,024 signed 32-bit integers and returns 1 for a repeated value, 0 otherwise, or -1 for invalid values or lengths. Each port sorts a private copy with portable heapsort.

The pinned C LeetCode 2222 source counts 010 and 101 subsequences with two linear passes. The shared contract represents the binary string as ASCII values, bounds its length to 4096, and the nine portable ports count both patterns in O(n) time and O(1) space.

The pinned C LeetCode 223 source computes the sum of two rectangle areas minus their positive-area intersection. The shared contract uses eight bounded signed coordinates and valid nonempty rectangles. The nine portable ports use integer clipping and return a signed 64-bit union area in O(1) time and space.

The pinned C LeetCode 2256 source sums the array, then scans all prefixes and compares truncated integer averages for the prefix and remaining suffix; a missing suffix average is zero. The shared contract bounds nonnegative values to 0..100000 and length to 100000, preserving integer division and first-index tie behavior. All nine ports use two linear scans and constant auxiliary space.

The pinned C LeetCode 226 source recursively swaps each node’s left and right links. The shared indexed-tree contract serializes the mirrored node table in little-endian signed 64-bit triplets so all nine portable implementations can be compared exactly.

The pinned C LeetCode 2270 source sums the array, then scans each valid prefix split and counts positions where the left sum is at least the remaining right sum. The shared contract bounds signed values to -100000..100000 and length to 2..100000; all nine portable ports use 64-bit sums and two linear scans with constant auxiliary space.

The pinned C LeetCode 2279 source computes each bag’s remaining capacity from its capacity and current rocks, sorts those deficits, then greedily spends additional rocks on the smallest deficits first. The shared packed contract preserves the budget, bag count, capacities, and rocks; it bounds the bag count to 8191 so the identical fixed work array fits below C3’s 64 KiB stack-object limit. All nine ports compute deficits, heap-sort them, and scan the affordable prefix.

The pinned C LeetCode 230 source performs recursive inorder DFS, decrements k at each node, and returns as soon as the rank reaches zero. The benchmark preserves this early exit over unique-value BSTs, extends the node-value contract to include zero as allowed by LeetCode, and limits trees to 1,023 nodes for the portable indexed-tree ABI. All nine ports pass the independent inorder oracle.

The pinned C LeetCode 2304 source uses row-by-row dynamic programming: for each next column it minimizes the prior path cost plus the current grid value and the value-indexed move cost, then adds the final-row cell value. The shared packed contract uses rectangular grids and a complete move-cost table, with each dimension bounded to 32. All nine ports keep two column-sized DP rows and run in O(rows * columns^2) time.
The pinned C LeetCode source checks positivity and applies the standard n & (n - 1) power-of-two predicate, matching the existing signed 64-bit benchmark semantics on the source's integer domain.

The pinned C LeetCode 234 source uses slow/fast pointers, reverses the second half of the linked list, and compares values. The shared ABI represents the values in order as a read-only array, so the benchmark compares from both ends with O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space while preserving the palindrome result. The contract accepts up to 100,000 digits in 0..9, extends empty input as a palindrome, and returns -1 for invalid inputs. All nine ports passed 10,656 oracle arrays and 11 workload cases.

The pinned C LeetCode 236 source builds root-to-target paths for p and q, then returns the last node in their longest common prefix. The shared indexed-tree contract returns the ancestor table index and requires distinct, uniquely valued targets. All nine ports pass 23,424 valid and malformed packed-tree cases against an independent parent-set oracle and record all six workload cases; see build/lowest_common_ancestor/verification.json.

The pinned C LeetCode 24 source recursively rewires adjacent linked-list nodes and leaves an unpaired final node in place. The shared bounded array contract serializes the same pairwise order transformation as signed 32-bit values.

The pinned C LeetCode 242 source counts lowercase ASCII letters in each input string and compares the two 26-entry frequency tables. The shared packed-array contract validates lowercase ASCII values, string lengths through 1,024, and an exact packed length; it returns 1 for matching frequencies, 0 otherwise, and -1 for malformed input.

The pinned C LeetCode 2482 source counts ones in each row and column, but uses the opposite dimension when deriving zero counts on rectangular matrices. The benchmark follows the stated formula onesRow[r] + onesColumn[c] - zerosRow[r] - zerosColumn[c], accepts matrices up to 100,000 cells, and serializes signed 32-bit little-endian results. All nine portable ports run in O(rows * columns) time and reuse the output buffer for row/column counts instead of using architecture-specific optimizations.

The pinned C LeetCode 2501 source marks values present in a set, memoizes square-chain lengths, and takes the maximum chain with at least two values. The shared contract accepts 2 through 100,000 values in 2..100,000 and uses a 400,004-byte caller workspace for portable presence and memo states, avoiding large stack arrays and per-language allocation differences. All nine ports use the same O(n + maxValue) recurrence and leave input unchanged.

The pinned C LeetCode 26 source uses a write index to compact an ascending array in place and returns the unique-prefix length. The shared bounded contract serializes that prefix as signed 32-bit values and leaves the input buffer unchanged.

The pinned C LeetCode 268 source subtracts the observed array sum from the arithmetic-series sum for 0 through n. The shared contract validates distinct inputs in [0,n], permits the empty array, and returns its unique missing value.

The pinned C LeetCode 27 source uses a write index to remove every matching target in place and returns the survivor count. The shared contract accepts a target followed by signed 32-bit values and serializes stable survivors to a separate output buffer.

The pinned C LeetCode 274 source sorts citations in place and scans from largest to smallest. The shared array-scalar ABI is read-only, so the benchmark preserves the H-index definition with an upper-midpoint binary search over h and a count of citations >= h. The contract accepts 0 through 5,000 values in 0..1,000, returns 0 for empty input, and returns -1 for invalid input. All nine ports use O(n log(min(n, 1000))) time, O(1) auxiliary space, and do not mutate input.

The pinned C LeetCode 278 source performs lower-bound binary search using an external isBadVersion API. The benchmark represents that monotone predicate with a first_bad input and tests middle >= first_bad, preserving the O(log n) algorithm and avoiding an external dependency. The shared contract supports version counts through 2^31-1, validates the predicate boundary, and uses an overflow-safe midpoint. All nine portable ports passed 9,105 oracle pairs and 15 workload cases.

The pinned C LeetCode 28 file defines strStr twice: an initial direct character scan with O(mn) worst-case work, followed by a KMP implementation with O(m+n) work. The KMP implementation aliases the existing KMP benchmark, and the direct scan is recorded separately as str_str_brute_force.

The pinned C LeetCode 283 source stably compacts nonzero values toward the front, then fills the remaining positions with zero. The shared contract keeps the input read-only to the caller and returns the same-length result in a separate little-endian signed 32-bit buffer.

The pinned C LeetCode 287 source sorts the input and scans adjacent values, which mutates the array and misses the problem's linear-time, constant-space follow-up. The benchmark follows the official contract with Floyd's cycle-entry algorithm, accepts up to 100,000 values plus the repeated entry, and leaves input unchanged. All nine ports passed 17,733 exhaustive/randomized/frequency-oracle arrays and 12 workload cases, including the maximum 100,001-value input.

The pinned C LeetCode 29 source doubles the divisor to subtract large multiples while keeping working values nonpositive. The shared contract widens signed 32-bit values, truncates toward zero, and saturates the quotient to the signed 32-bit range.

The pinned C LeetCode 3 source contains an O(n) last-seen-index implementation and a separate brute-force duplicate definition; the O(n) implementation returns the longest substring length. It is reviewed as a LeetCode-number alias of the alphabetically named benchmark.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 32 implementation. It uses a memoized endpoint recurrence to find the longest well-formed contiguous parenthesis substring. The shared contract encodes parentheses as ASCII values in a bounded signed 64-bit array; the nine portable ports evaluate the recurrence bottom-up to avoid recursion-depth dependence.

The pinned C LeetCode 344 source reverses a char array in place by swapping its left and right endpoints while moving inward. The shared byte-array contract validates values 0..255 and adapts mutation to a separate output buffer while preserving the same two-pointer swaps.

The pinned C LeetCode 35 file contains two conflicting definitions of searchInsert. The first, iterative definition performs binary search; the benchmark follows it for strictly increasing signed 32-bit arrays and returns the lower-bound insertion index.
The pinned C LeetCode 367 source reports whether a nonnegative integer is a perfect square; its loop implementation shares the canonical exact square predicate.

The pinned C LeetCode 37 source intends row, column, and 3x3-box occupancy tracking with recursive backtracking, but it recurses before writing the trial digit into the board, so it revisits the same blank. The nine ports implement the intended row-major search with the digit placed before recursion and removed after a failed branch. The independent verifier confirms unique solutions and checks all nine ports.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 38 implementation. It starts with the term "1" and repeatedly emits each run length followed by its digit. The shared contract uses a bounded one-based index of 1 through 19 so all terms fit the portable 256-byte scalar-output ABI, and defines invalid-index and output-capacity behavior.

The pinned C LeetCode 387 source counts byte frequencies and returns the first unique character index. The shared contract uses the problem domain of lowercase ASCII letters, represented as integer byte values.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 389 implementation. It sums the character codes in both lowercase strings and returns target sum minus source sum; correctness relies on the target being a permutation with one extra character. The shared contract packs both explicit lengths and byte arrays into the scalar-array ABI, then uses the same sum method in nine portable ports.

The pinned Ruby source generates the Collatz trajectory beginning with the input and ending at 1, then formats it as text. The shared collatz_sequence contract represents those same values as portable little-endian integers for positive bounded inputs.

The pinned TheAlgorithms/Ruby source sorts a copy, skips duplicate first values, and uses a two-pointer search to enumerate unique zero-sum triplets. The nine target-language ports preserve that O(n^2) search and input immutability, with a portable heap sort and explicit little-endian triplet encoding. The local input bound is 257 (rather than LeetCode’s 3,000) so the conservative maximum output fits the existing byte-output ABI. All nine ports passed 4,175 oracle inputs and 12 workload records.

The pinned C LeetCode 4 source merges two already sorted arrays before selecting the median. This is algorithmically distinct from the one-array median benchmark, which insertion-sorts a single unsorted array. The cross-language contract packs two sorted signed-32-bit arrays and returns twice their exact statistical median.

The pinned C LeetCode source returns the sum of values at leaf nodes that are left children, recursively traversing both subtrees. The shared contract uses a bounded indexed tree and signed values in [-1000, 1000], with portable recursive ports in all nine target languages.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 42 implementation. It computes suffix maximum heights and a running prefix maximum, then sums trapped water, matching trapped_rainwater. Its source assumes a nonempty array; the shared benchmark contract defines empty input as zero and handles it safely.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 434 source. It counts transitions from ASCII space to non-space, treating only space as a delimiter. The shared contract uses an explicit-length nonzero ASCII byte array; all nine portable ports preserve the transition-count algorithm.

The pinned C LeetCode 442 source sorts the input, then scans adjacent values and emits each duplicate once; the problem contract guarantees each value appears at most twice. The shared benchmark returns those values in ascending order, encodes them as little-endian signed 32-bit values, and defines bounded input and output-capacity behavior. All nine ports passed 32,482 oracle inputs and recorded 12 workload cases.

The pinned C LeetCode 45 source explores reachable array indices in breadth-first layers, deduplicating enqueued positions with a visited array, and returns the first layer reaching the last index. The portable benchmark preserves BFS using one FIFO queue, visited flags, and per-index distances.

The pinned C LeetCode 461 source counts differing bits of two nonnegative signed 32-bit values. On this domain, zero-extending each value to the shared unsigned 64-bit hamming_distance contract preserves the result.
The pinned C LeetCode 476 source constructs a mask through the most significant input bit and returns the same significant-bit complement as candidate 1009.
The pinned C LeetCode 485 source counts contiguous ones in a binary array. Its shared binary-input contract is the same as max_consecutive_ones, so this candidate is an alias.

The pinned TheAlgorithms/C LeetCode 5 source describes center expansion for odd and even palindromes, but allocates only sizeof(pointer) bytes for its result. The benchmark preserves the O(n^2) center-expansion algorithm with caller-provided output storage. Its contract follows the official 1-to-1,000 ASCII alphanumeric input domain, returns the leftmost longest substring on ties, and uses -1/-2 for invalid input/insufficient capacity. All nine portable ports are checked against an independent interval dynamic-programming oracle.

The pinned C LeetCode 50 source computes powers by recursive repeated squaring and reciprocates negative exponents, with a special case for INT32_MIN. The nine ports preserve the repeated-squaring operation order under the shared binary64 base and signed 32-bit exponent contract.
The pinned C LeetCode 509 source computes the zero-based Fibonacci value with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1.

Inspected both detectCapitalUse definitions in the pinned C LeetCode 520 source. The first counts uppercase letters in O(n); the second invokes an all-uppercase scan for every uppercase byte after the first, giving O(n^2) worst-case work. The original file repeats the function definition, so each approach is cataloged separately with matching semantics and portable nine-language ports.
The pinned C LeetCode 53 source uses Kadane’s recurrence for the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous subarray. It has the same objective as maximum_subarray and is recorded as an alias.

The pinned C LeetCode 540 source uses binary search on pair alignment in a sorted array where one value occurs once and all others occur twice. The shared contract preserves this precondition and returns the unique value.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 561 implementation. It sorts the input with qsort and sums every even-positioned value. The shared contract bounds values to signed 32-bit integers and requires an even length; nine portable ports use the same in-place heapsort procedure on a local copy.

The pinned C LeetCode 567 source maintains pattern-versus-window letter-count differences and a mismatch count while sliding across the text. The pinned JavaScript PermutationinString source also compares 26-letter frequency windows. The shared contract packs lowercase ASCII strings, limits each to 1,024 characters, and returns whether a permutation occurs as a contiguous substring; all nine ports use a fixed 26-entry table and portable integer operations.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 6 implementation. It emits the first and last rows with a fixed 2*(rows-1) gap and alternates complementary gaps for interior rows. The benchmark preserves that row-by-row ordering, uses an explicit byte-array ABI, and defines bounded ASCII-letter, empty-input, invalid-row, and output-capacity behavior.

The pinned C LeetCode 617 source recursively creates a new tree, adding values where both inputs have nodes and copying a lone node value otherwise. The scalar predicate agrees with the existing kaprekar_number benchmark on positive inputs; it returns true for zero, unlike that benchmark contract, so the scalar mapping is restricted to its positive domain. The separate range benchmark preserves Java's inclusion of zero and one.

The mixed generic knapsack filename candidate is also an alias for its 0/1 variants; its two C++ fractional-knapsack files are tracked under fractional_knapsack.

The pinned C# iterator yields 1, 2, 2, seeds its queue with run length 2, and emits alternating 1s and 2s according to queued run lengths. The benchmark exposes zero-based terms 0..63, preserving the sequence while bounding the packed representation.
The pinned C# KolakoskiSequence2 is an alternate lazy generator of the same 1,2 self-run-length sequence. It maps to the shared zero-based Kolakoski sequence contract.

The pinned Go predicate returns false for n<=0, then sums factorials of decimal digits and compares with n. It agrees with the shared checker on signed-int32 inputs.

Nine ports and a workload are present; runtime verification remains pending.

The pinned Python source computes the Liouville function λ(n)=(-1)^Ω(n), where Ω counts prime factors with multiplicity; λ(1)=+1 and nonpositive inputs are invalid. The contract bounds n to 1..2,147,483,647. This is distinct from the Möbius function μ: for example λ(4)=+1 while μ(4)=0.

The pinned Java method uses two dynamic-programming states per endpoint: a strict rise extends a falling subsequence and a strict fall extends a rising subsequence. It initializes each state and the overall result to 1, so its empty-input result is also 1; the benchmark preserves that source edge behavior. The local contract bounds values to signed int32 and length to 512.

The pinned Java source uses O(n^2) dynamic programming indexed by endpoint and adjacent difference to find the longest arithmetic subsequence. The benchmark bounds length to 64 and values to ±1,000,000, keeping differences exact and fixed storage bounded. Ports use max-merge for repeated endpoint/difference states, which preserves the source result. This is distinct from strictly increasing subsequences and contiguous increasing runs.
The pinned Java source returns the longest common prefix of an array of ASCII strings. The benchmark sorts internal indices for deterministic concatenated output without changing the input array.

The pinned C++, Dart, Java, JavaScript, Python, R, Julia, Kotlin, Rust, C, and TypeScript sources implement longest common subsequence. The pinned C++, Java, Rust, and Zig sources compute a strictly increasing subsequence; the Rust source returns a sequence while this benchmark standardizes its length. The pinned Java implementation uses gap-table dynamic programming to find a longest palindromic substring, a distinct strategy from candidate 5's center expansion. The benchmark returns the rightmost longest substring on ties, matching the source's update rule.

The pinned Java method tests bases in ascending order starting at 2 and returns the first base in which the nonnegative number is palindromic. This is distinct from fixed-base palindrome predicates and decimal string palindrome checks.

The pinned C++ and C++-1 mirrors, C#, Python, and Zig implementations provide LRU page-cache behavior. The pinned C# source yields Lucas values 2, 1, then advances by previous+current, exactly matching zero-based L(0)=2, L(1)=1. The existing Lucas benchmark supports indices 0..90; this is a bounded scalar term view of the same lazy BigInteger sequence.

The pinned Java, JavaScript, Python, Ruby, Rust, and Solidity files all concern the Lucas sequence, but use different index conventions and methods. The benchmark uses exact zero-based recurrence with L(0)=2 and L(1)=1; Java’s one-based entry point is normalized, and the Ruby floating-point formula is known to disagree at indices 0 and 1. Recursive and iterative methods are tracked as separate benchmarks.

The pinned Java implementation is an iterative position test whose counter starts at 2 and increments by exactly one after each division step. The benchmark preserves that exact method, including its difference from standard lucky-number sieve membership (for example, 15 is false), on positive inputs 1..1,000,000. Boolean results 0/1 cannot collide with the -1 invalid sentinel.

The pinned C#, Go, Java, and Python implementations agree on even-length decimal digit sequences: double alternating digits from the left, subtract nine when a doubled digit exceeds nine, and check divisibility by ten. The package bounds the shared domain to 2..64 digits and excludes odd lengths, malformed strings, and non-digits where source behavior differs.

The pinned C++ sources define a magic number as a positive integer whose repeated decimal digit sums reach one, using the equivalent n % 9 == 1 check. The benchmark uses the positive-number definition consistently across signed 64-bit inputs, returning false for zero and negatives.

The pinned Python source computes magnetic flux as the field-area product times cosine of the angle in radians, rounded to one decimal place. The bounded package preserves the source SI units and operation/domain rules.

The pinned Java method returns every distinct int whose frequency is at least floor(n/2), not a single strict majority element. HashMap iteration order is unspecified; the benchmark normalizes returned values to ascending signed-i32 order.

The pinned Python implementation generalizes Boyer-Moore voting for a threshold k. With k=2 it returns the strict majority element, matching the canonical benchmark; the generalized thresholds are outside this benchmark contract.

The pinned C# source yields the first 17 change-count terms for unlimited 1-, 2-, 5-, and 10-cent coins, then uses its stated seven-offset recurrence. The benchmark indexes terms for amounts 0 through 128; the nine ports preserve the seed values and left-to-right recurrence order.

The pinned Python source requires nonnegative intensity and angle in inclusive [0,360], then computes `initial_intensity * (cos(radians(angle)) ** 2)`. The benchmark selects bounded integer inputs from the float API, preserves the source guards and operation order, and maps invalid ABI cases to -1e300; the source itself raises ValueError for invalid physical inputs.

The pinned F#, Java, Python, and Rust sources use Manacher radius reuse to return a longest palindromic substring. The bounded ASCII alphanumeric domain avoids marker collisions and empty-input failures; the shared leftmost tie rule normalizes Rust’s rightmost tie choice and the F# mirror-bound defect.

The pinned C++ and C++-1 Manacher implementations use transformed-string radius reuse and select the leftmost maximum. Their substring semantics match the canonical package on the bounded ASCII alphanumeric domain.

The pinned R source uses Manacher radius reuse and selects the leftmost longest palindrome. Its lowercasing occurs only in the command-line wrapper; the shared ASCII alphanumeric contract matches the canonical package.
The pinned C# method uses Manacher radius reuse and strict-greater tie updates, matching the canonical package’s leftmost maximum on the bounded ASCII alphanumeric domain.

The pinned Python functions compute the sum of absolute coordinate differences after validating nonempty, equal-length numeric vectors. The benchmark uses a bounded dimension and integer-coordinate subset, preserving exact n-dimensional L1 distance and remaining distinct from Euclidean distance.

The pinned Python source exports energy_from_mass(mass)=mass*c**2 and mass_from_energy(energy)=energy/c**2 using c=299792458 m/s; each rejects negative inputs and accepts zero. The benchmark exposes both operations through an operation selector and bounds the nonnegative integer input to 1,000,000,000. All nine ports preserve the operation-specific formula and invalid-input behavior.

The pinned C-Sharp generator computes floor(n*(n+2)*(2n+1)/8) at zero-based indices. The benchmark follows the executable expression, bounds the index to signed-i64-safe intermediates, and does not substitute its differing documentation formula.

The pinned C++ sources use a memoized top-down recurrence with a small fixed dimension table; Python includes bottom-up tabulation and cached recursion. The benchmark contract uses bottom-up matrix-chain dynamic programming on positive dimensions and bounds the chain and dimensions so signed 64-bit costs are safe.

The pinned Java and TypeScript sources implement rectangular matrix products; JavaScript also computes the same dot products but its dimension check only accepts square output and fails on one-row inputs. The package uses square matrices of size 2..8 with bounded integer cells, which is the common valid domain and keeps every result exact.

The pinned Go and Lua variadic max functions seed from the first value and replace it only on a strict comparison, so ties retain the earliest input. The package preserves that behavior for nonempty signed-i32 arrays.

The pinned Ruby function scans the decimal string left to right, changes the first character exactly equal to 6 into 9, and returns; it yields nil when no 6 occurs. The benchmark makes the challenge domain explicit (positive values with only 6/9 digits), where this means changing the most significant 6. It maps nil and out-of-domain values to -1. No equivalent local benchmark was found.

The pinned JavaScript and PHP sources both return the most frequent character. The benchmark restricts inputs to lowercase ASCII with a unique maximum, so JavaScript's case-sensitive insertion-order scan and PHP's lowercase byte-count plus descending sort return the same character. The JavaScript ignore-pattern option is not used; PHP's empty-string and "0" exceptions are outside the valid domain.

The pinned JavaScript source uses a sliding window to count consecutive ones. The shared benchmark contract uses binary arrays; its scan returns the same longest run while validating the input domain.

The pinned Python source recursively compares left, cross, and right value pairs, preserving its strict tie-selection order. It permits the same index for both values, so decreasing arrays return a zero-difference pair; this differs from stock-profit benchmarks.

The pinned C, Dart, Haskell, Java, Python, and Ruby sources share insert, inspect-maximum, and extract-maximum operations. The contract restricts keys to signed 32-bit values and normalizes language-specific empty-heap behavior to INT64_MIN; duplicate-key layout is not observable.

The pinned Ruby implementation uses first-seen word counts and a frequency-only max heap with strict comparisons, matching the Python top_k_frequent_words behavior and its heap-layout-dependent tie order on the shared bounded domain.

The pinned Python, JavaScript, and Java implementations use the rolling exclude/include recurrence for non-adjacent selection. The shared nonnegative domain permits selecting nothing, matching the canonical package and avoiding the Java negative-singleton mismatch and JavaScript empty-array behavior.

The pinned JavaScript source tracks the three largest and two smallest values in one pass, then compares the two candidate products. The bounded integer contract keeps both products exact and preserves -1 as a valid result; invalid inputs use the INT64_MIN ABI sentinel.

The pinned Python routine returns 0 for empty input and otherwise tracks maximum and minimum products ending at each position, swapping their roles for negative values. The bounded ports preserve the recurrence; the Java/Ruby maximum_product_subarray source is a separate contract.

The pinned Python source uses divide and conquer and returns the selected start, end, and sum. Its sum objective is benchmarked with the same nonempty contract as maximum_subarray while preserving divide and conquer as a distinct algorithm strategy.
The pinned Python implementation defaults to allow_empty_subarrays=False and uses Kadane’s recurrence, matching the nonempty maximum-subarray contract.

The pinned Java source sums the first k elements, initializes the maximum from that window so all-negative inputs work, then slides by adding the entering value and removing the leaving value. k=0 returns zero; positive k larger than the array and negative k are normalized to -1 by the contract. This fixed-length window operation is distinct from unrestricted maximum-subarray.

The pinned Python source and JavaScript fixed-window source implement the same rolling contiguous-window maximum sum. The shared contract requires 1 <= k <= n and bounded signed values; k=0 is excluded because the Python and JavaScript sources differ there.

The pinned JavaScript MaxSumSubarrayFixed source implements the same rolling fixed-window maximum sum as the canonical Python source. The alias contract requires k>=1, excluding the source-language difference at k=0.

The pinned Java method returns the first signed-i32 operand when it is greater than or equal to the second, otherwise the second; equality therefore returns the shared value. The package preserves this pairwise maximum contract.

The pinned Ruby and Rust implementations compute the greatest sum of a nonempty contiguous subarray with Kadane’s recurrence. The Ruby source uses an Integer array and Rust uses an i64 slice; both have the same objective and empty-subarray behavior.

The pinned Java source maximizes sums over fixed-size windows only when every value is distinct. The benchmark preserves its zero-initialized maximum, including when no distinct window exists or every valid sum is negative.

The pinned Java maximum-sum-of-non-adjacent-elements implementation uses the same rolling dynamic-programming recurrence as the canonical package. The shared nonnegative domain makes its nonempty input results agree.

The pinned C++, Go, JavaScript, Python, and Rust implementations compute standard MD5 over bytes. Go, JavaScript, and Rust expose digest bytes; Python returns lowercase hexadecimal and the benchmark normalizes it to 16 raw bytes. The mirrored C++ endian helper is correct on little-endian hosts but skips the needed conversion on big-endian hosts, so the portable contract specifies byte order directly.
The pinned C, Go, and PHP mean sources compute sum divided by count and map to the canonical average benchmark. The shared contract makes fractional output binary64 and bounds the signed-i64 sum.

The pinned JavaScript method computes the arithmetic mean through AverageMean.js, then returns the average absolute difference from that mean. The benchmark uses nonempty bounded integer arrays so the mean sum is exact in binary64, and maps malformed/empty source exceptions to a sentinel. All nine target-language ABI implementations compile and link.

The pinned Rust mae_loss sums absolute differences for zipped prediction/actual values and divides by predicted length. The benchmark preserves this mean absolute error formula on equal-length bounded integer arrays and maps malformed inputs to a sentinel. All nine target-language ABI implementations compile and link.

The pinned JavaScript source sums squared expected-minus-predicted differences and divides by the expected-list length; unequal list lengths throw, while empty lists yield NaN. The benchmark uses equal-length bounded integer arrays, maps malformed and empty packed inputs to a sentinel, and keeps the maximum sum below 2^53. All nine target-language ABI implementations compile and link.

The pinned Rust mse_loss sums squared differences for zipped prediction/actual values and divides by predicted length. On equal-length inputs this is the same mean-squared-error formula as the canonical benchmark; the local contract bounds both arrays and requires matching lengths.

The pinned Java Means.java defines arithmetic, geometric, harmonic, and quadratic means. Arithmetic maps to the existing arithmetic_mean package; geometric maps to geometric_mean on the positive bounded subset, where the Java product-root formula agrees with the canonical package. The harmonic method returns n divided by the sum of reciprocals, and the quadratic method returns the square root of the average of squares; both now have dedicated nine-language packages.

Inspected the pinned C, Go, Java, Kotlin, Lua, and PHP sources. The C file is an interactive random-data demonstration and integer-divides the middle pair before storing into float; Go divides the two middle generic integer values before converting to float64; Java and Kotlin sort integer arrays but add the middle int values before conversion, which can overflow; Lua uses quickselect; and PHP sorts variadic numeric inputs. The shared contract is a nonempty array of signed 32-bit integers with exact statistical median semantics. To preserve half-integer results in the signed-64-bit scalar ABI, the result is encoded as twice the median. The nine portable read-only ports insertion-sort a bounded local copy.

The pinned Java source binary-searches a partition in the shorter sorted array and derives the matching partition in the longer array, returning the exact median in logarithmic search time. This differs algorithmically from C LeetCode 4's linear merge benchmark and maps to the dedicated partition-search package. The shared contract returns twice the median to preserve half-integer results exactly.

The pinned Python source orders adjacent pairs, merge-sorts pairs by their lower values, then builds a sorted chain by binary insertion of the pair upper values and an odd leftover. The two C++ copies describe a merge/insertion hybrid but the demo calls only insertion sort and comments out the hybrid call. The shared contract follows the Python pair-and-insert strategy, uses full-chain lower-bound insertion for duplicates, and sorts signed 64-bit arrays up to length 256.

The C implementation recursively merges inclusive ranges and allocates a fresh buffer per merge; C++ allocates two vectors per merge; Rust provides top-down and bottom-up variants with temporary vectors. The local benchmark fixes stable bottom-up merging with a reusable scratch buffer allocated outside timing.

The pinned C source uses iterative bottom-up merge passes, but its temporary array holds only 50 int values and its demo performs interactive I/O. The shared benchmark sorts signed 64-bit values in place up to length 1024, uses one fixed scratch array, and keeps I/O outside the timed call. Ports merge ties from the left; the upstream C example takes the right value on equal keys, which is unobservable for this scalar integer contract.

The pinned Java implementation recursively divides each list into halves and merges the sorted halves, matching the top-down merge strategy represented by merge_sorter. It creates sublists and recursively copies list tails during merging; the shared contract uses one reusable scratch buffer for signed 64-bit values.
The pinned Dart source compares the current nodes from both ascending lists and links the lower value into the result. It implements the same merged-value semantics as C LeetCode 21.

The pinned C-Sharp MergeSorter recursively splits the array, sorts each half, and merges with left-first tie handling, allocating subarrays at each split. The shared benchmark preserves the top-down recursion and stable result while using one fixed scratch array allocated per call, with signed 64-bit inputs capped at length 1024. It remains distinct from the bottom-up merge_sort and merge_sort_nr benchmarks.

The pinned Python source recursively adds overlapping node values and reuses a lone node when the other tree is absent. It mutates tree1, while canonical C candidate 617 allocates a fresh output tree; under the packed pure-output contract their merged shape and values are identical, so this is an alias of merge_two_binary_trees.

The pinned Python helper constructs a sorted result from both input lists rather than using the linear two-cursor merge. Its output semantics match C LeetCode 21 on the shared sorted-input domain; the method difference is documented in the benchmark guide.
The pinned JavaScript source walks both sorted lists and appends the lower current value to a new list. Its output semantics match C LeetCode 21 on the shared sorted-input domain.

The pinned Python and Lua sources recursively divide and merge halves. The Go file contains recursive Merge plus iterative and parallel alternatives; the shared candidate mapping follows the recursive top-down strategy, represented by merge_sorter.

The pinned Julia predicate repeatedly divides n+1 by two, then checks that the remainder is one before calling prime_check(n). The package preserves that candidate-value check on 0..INT32_MAX; zero and one are false, while negatives and values above the bound return -1. Negative -1 would make the upstream reduction loop non-terminating, so the benchmark wrapper rejects it. Exponent-based Lucas-Lehmer routines use a different input contract.

The pinned Rust `mex_using_sort` copies and sorts the input, then finds the smallest missing nonnegative value. The benchmark preserves the read-only input and sorting approach; it does not use the same file’s set-based alternative.

The pinned Java source advances slow by one node and fast by two, returning the second middle node for even-length lists and null for an empty list. That matches the canonical LeetCode 876 benchmark's middle-node semantics; the shared successor-index contract represents the returned node by its index and defines explicit malformed-input behavior.

The pinned Java source special-cases radius zero as the center point. For positive radii it begins at `(radius,0)`, appends all eight symmetric points in a fixed order with duplicates retained, then updates the midpoint parameter while x>y. The benchmark preserves this exact point trace under bounded center and radius inputs.

The pinned Java source uses two midpoint decision regions, emits four symmetric points in a fixed order without deduplication, and handles zero axes as a point or an ascending horizontal/vertical line. The benchmark preserves these degenerate cases, point ordering, and duplicates under bounded center and axis inputs.

The pinned C++ implementation chooses random witness bases, while the Rust implementation accepts a caller-supplied base list and returns a compositeness witness. The shared contract uses fixed bases [2, 3, 5, 7] and returns 1 for prime or 0 for composite. The Rust source notes these bases are deterministic below 3,215,031,751, covering the selected signed 32-bit domain. Negative values and values below 2 return 0; values above the signed 32-bit maximum return -1.

The pinned Go and Lua variadic min functions seed from the first value and replace it only on a strict comparison, so ties retain the earliest input. The package preserves that behavior for nonempty signed-i32 arrays.

The pinned Dart function initializes a DP array to `1_000_000_000_000`, sets position zero to 0, then scans each earlier position for every destination and relaxes reachable jumps. The package preserves that quadratic recurrence and sentinel; empty input is excluded because the source indexes position zero.

The pinned Java source returns -1 when k exceeds the array length, returns zero for k=0, and otherwise slides a fixed-size window while retaining its minimum sum. The bounded contract keeps Java int32 intermediate arithmetic safe and excludes negative k.

The pinned Java method returns the first signed-i32 operand when it is less than or equal to the second, otherwise the second; equality therefore returns the shared value. The package preserves this pairwise minimum contract.

The pinned JavaScript, Python, and Rust sources compute a top-left to bottom-right minimum path using only right and down moves; their table/mutation strategies differ but the recurrence agrees. Python mutates its matrix without changing the return value. Rust takes `Vec<Vec<usize>>`, so its upstream domain is nonnegative; the benchmark also covers signed i32 inputs for Python, JavaScript, and the portable ports. The common matrix shape and invalid-input behavior are standardized by the package.

The pinned Python source uses a shrinking sliding window to find the shortest contiguous range whose sum reaches the target. Positive values keep that method valid; the contract excludes zero-target and negative-value cases.

The pinned Python source uses bottom-up dynamic programming to return the minimum number of square terms whose sum is n. It special-cases zero to return 1 even though the DP base is zero; positive inputs minimize 1+dp[n-j*j]. The benchmark bounds n to 0..4096 and maps invalid values to -1. This count is distinct from a perfect-square predicate or a sum of squares.

The pinned Python source initializes a table with n+1, sets table[1]=0, then scans i upward and relaxes i+1, 2*i, and 3*i in that order when in range. The bounded package preserves the exact forward tabulation result.

The pinned C# Distance method validates order>=1 and equal point lengths, then computes the same generalized Minkowski formula as the Python source. The package p=3..6 bounded contract is a shared subdomain; p=1 and p=2 remain covered by their dedicated Manhattan and Euclidean benchmarks.

The pinned Python and C# sources validate positive order and equal point dimensions, then compute (sum(abs(a-b)^p))^(1/p). The package bounds p to 3..6 and coordinates/dimensions so integer intermediates are exact and safe; all workload outputs are exact roots or zero for the exact-comparison runner.
